speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked if we will review the safe management measures (SMMs), given that we have passed the peak of the Omicron wave.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We did not declare a Freedom Day nor did we declare the pandemic to be over, as some countries did.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Taking a cautious step-by-step approach has served us well throughout the pandemic and we will continue to do so.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That said, we were able to make this decisive move as we observed that the number of daily cases had been steadily declining in recent weeks.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: More importantly, the number of severe cases needing to be hospitalised had also declined.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is in this context that the Multi-MinistryTask Force (MTF) assessed the further easing of our SMMs and resumption of many normal activities to be appropriate.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These relaxations will likely cause an uptick in daily cases, which we should be able to ride through without any major changes to our public health posture.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Once cases subside further, we will consider further easing of the SMMs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This can include reviewing distancing rules between tables in F&B settings that Mr Liang Eng Hwa specifically raised, and I want to assure Mr Liang that I am aware that one metre versus 80 centimetres makes a huge difference to F&B establishments.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It also makes a huge difference in terms of transmission.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, we have to weigh the costs and benefits.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will also review TraceTogether, SafeEntry, as well as Vaccination-Differentiated Safe Management Measures (VDS) which various Members have asked about.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On TraceTogether, and in response to Ms Hazel Poa and Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, MOH no longer relies on TraceTogether for contact tracing for the general public.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Cases who self-tested positive and go on to Protocol 2 do not upload their TraceTogether data, and we rely on them to do the responsible thing to inform their contacts to self-monitor.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, there is really no need to compare the data between self-reporting and TraceTogether because, having vaccinated the vast majority of our population and being determined to live with COVID-19, we have passed that stage of the pandemic where we contact trace every case.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Having said that, agencies that look after more vulnerable sectors, such as schools or preschools, continue to use TraceTogether for contact tracing.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Further, the aggregated statistics generated by TraceTogether and SafeEntry can give us a good idea of the settings that are more susceptible to transmission of the COVID-19 virus.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, on the whole, the costs and benefits of TraceTogether change as we make further progress in living with COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MTF will, therefore, review its relevance and application to stand it down when it is no longer needed, while maintaining the capability to restart it should we encounter a more dangerous variant of concern.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For SafeEntry and VDS, I will address them together because they are closely related.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Today, SafeEntry is the most convenient way to check the vaccination status of an individual entering premises.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If we decide to do away with VDS, then there is no need for SafeEntry.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Even as we know that the Omicron variant is less severe than Delta, unvaccinated or non-fully vaccinated persons are still a lot more likely to fall very ill if they are infected.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: While the patient load at our public hospitals has eased, hospitals are still very busy.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: With the recent easing of SMMs and the resumption of visitors to hospitals starting today, workload will go up for our healthcare workers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Individuals who choose not to be vaccinated impose a cost, sometimes a significant one, on our hospitals in terms of workload, businesses in operating SafeEntry checks and enforcement agencies in conducting checks.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When we are sure that the situation in hospitals is stable and improving, we will review the VDS and consider if we can reduce the number of settings or remove it completely.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Then, it will be a matter of individual responsibility of these non-fully vaccinated individuals to take precautions to avoid high transmission settings, or better still, change their mind and get vaccinated.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is the objective set out by MTF last year and we are making good progress, as a country.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It does not mean we treat COVID-19 as if it is not there.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is, in fact, the opposite, because endemicity means the disease is constantly there, circulating at a rate that is more predictable and not likely to disrupt normal lives.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Like Influenza, which kills tens of thousands of people every year, we will need to continue to take precaution and adopt appropriate SMMs in order to manage the risk and damage from COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We are still some way to treating COVID-19 as an endemic disease, because the virus is still circulating around the world and evolving.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The virus continues to spread widely in other countries, especially among those whose people are not well vaccinated, leading to significant evolutionary pressure.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There is, therefore, still a risk of it mutating into something more dangerous, into a variant of concern.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, can I ask the Minister, from an equity standpoint, does it make sense to inconvenience the 96.5% of the population, just so that we can deter the 3.5% unvaccinated from entering the premises?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Does it really make a difference in terms of the public health outcomes?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Or is it just a move to basically disincentivise those unvaccinated from going there or to nudge them to get vaccinated?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I will answer the Member's questions in a straightforward way.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So many of us are doing so much to protect that 3.5%.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Is it, therefore, to protect public health outcomes?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As I have explained, hospitals are not out of the woods.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I just visited Ng Teng Fong General Hospital this morning.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We are prepared to gather together without safe distancing, take off our masks when we are outdoors.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In the hospitals, it is still a crisis situation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Every day, we have hundreds of people coming to the emergency department.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Many of them with chronic illnesses, some infected, but they do not know about it.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But that is the outcome of two over years of focusing on COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, while we understand it is not exactly an equitable situation when you look at businesses, you do not want, at this point, to add workload to our healthcare workers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, I will say the fair thing to do – we are just coming down the slope of the transmission wave.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, I do not see how the number of vaccinated people will go up.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The question that many people have asked is, when will all this end?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Like what Mr Liang Eng Hwa said, all these are at great inconvenience to the malls, because they have got to have manpower to man the entry and exit points of the malls.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It inconveniences the shoppers who have to go into the malls, because now they have fewer entry and exit points.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, surely, MOH ought to consider the principle of self-responsibility, which is that, those who choose to be unvaccinated have to take the consequences of their action.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I mean, if they choose to do so despite all our efforts to persuade them, then they have to take responsibility.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: At some point, the rules must be more relaxed.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The cost need not be incurred by businesses, and those who choose not to be vaccinated take the responsibility.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I just do not think it is now because have a care for healthcare workers at this point – they are still very busy.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Maybe go up marginally, but what we can wait for is for cases to go down further, for hospital situation to be eased; then, we will be in a position to review this and make the right decision.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And if I may just build off the questions that Members Liang Eng Hwa and Lim Biow Chuan have asked, I wonder if the Ministry is looking at specific milestones or quantitative triggers that would then bring about further easing and the evolution of measures, such as SafeEntry.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The MTF Co-Chairs have repeatedly been asked when is the next milestone, when is the next date, when is the next KPI to be reached and then we will open up further.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have always tried to avoid that approach that many countries took, that when we reach vaccination at X%, let us open up; on this day, let us open up.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And, so far, it has served us well.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We tighten up when we have to, to keep everyone safe and we also ease up when we can and letting economic and social activities resume as normally as possible.
